header.title: Sermonum Arianorum Fragmenta: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Monumenta Vetera Ad Arianorum Doctrinam
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp203.tmp203.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Letters and numerals beside words are footnote marks of the printed edition and are omitted. Read davit as dabit, secandum as secundum, honorificavit (Fragment II) as honorificabit, as the quoted verses require. Fragment I: 'lucentes non requirunt' seems corrupt; rendered tentatively 'shining, need nothing further'. 'si se nec aequalem nullius fecit' seems corrupt; rendered as if 'sicut nec aequalem ullius', 'just as he has made no one his equal'. 'in substitutione filii' is uncertain; rendered 'in the establishment of the Son'. 'in sua impropria nata substantia' is probably a misreading of 'propria' and is translated as 'own'. 'he has it and did not receive it' is the preacher's insertion into the quotation of John 5:26.

Fragment IV: after 'the one who commands' the text jumps to attributes of the Father ('and good, and alone having immortality'); something appears to have dropped out, marked [...]. 'Tales' read as talis, 'incomparabile' as incomparabili, 'in ficto' as in facto, 'grados' as gradus, 'secundum hanc sequentium' as sequentiam. The sentence 'quorum prior est Spiritus sanctus ... pronuntiatur' is syntactically loose in the Latin. The saying 'Ex verbo tuo manifestum quia justo ... justificaveris' (cf. Matt. 12:37) is garbled; the bracketed renderings are conjectural. The 'present psalm' is Psalm 14 (15) in the Latin numbering; the 'hundred and eleventh' is Ps. 111 (112).

Fragment V is badly damaged; lacunae are marked [...] and the connections between surviving phrases are uncertain. 'dealitatis' taken as 'deitatis' (divinity). In Fragment VI the sequence 'jubente Patre, quia filius hominis est' appears to skip text (it echoes John 5:27). The citation of John 5:29 is conflated as given: 'those who have done good... to the resurrection of judgement'. 'metallum ignis' is taken as a furnace or mine of fire; the reading may be corrupt. 'Filias' is read as 'Filius', 'jusso' as 'jussu', 'tringinta' as 'triginta', and 'suspitatorem' as 'sospitatorem'. In Fragment VII 'et iam' is read as 'et tamen', as in the parallel clauses, and 'linet' is taken as 'anoints'.

Fr. VIII: 'primitias ... sequentias' rendered 'first place ... following [place]'; the sense (first-fruits of honour vs. what follows) is uncertain. Fr. IX opens mid-word ('...ria'), perhaps [injuria] or [contra]ria; only 'defame us' is rendered. 'Soziphanes', leader of the Macedonians, is unidentified (possibly a corruption of a known name). Several scanning/spelling slips read as intended: 'discendi' = descendi, 'ni omne' = ut omne, 'per cum' = per eum, 'Ad ubi' = At ubi; in Fr. X 'qui' is supplied before 'dicunt'. The 'it is written' passages in Fr. X are deliberately inverted quotations, translated as given. In Fr. XI 'ei' (to him) in John 4 rendered 'to her' per the biblical context; the Latin has the ambiguous dative.

XIV: the printed text contains an intrusion from the editor's footnote, 'crea-terae. Nulla tamen videtur esse lacuna' ('...[the] other[s]. Nevertheless there seems to be no lacuna'), which interrupts 'creatum'; it has been left out. Superscript footnote letters (a, b, c...) omitted throughout. XIII: 'in notis' / 'in novis' read as 'in nobis'; 'dealitas' rendered 'deity'; 'innatum' taken as 'unbegotten'. XII: 'introivit', 'segregavit', 'transfiguravit' are perfects in this text (Vulgate has futures/present); translated as given. XV: 'in metallum ignis aeterni' literally 'to the mine of eternal fire' (condemnation ad metalla).

16.1: 'quid est' read as 'quia est', 'nan quia' as 'non quia'. 'Bithenus episcopus... et cognitus ad Papam' is unclear: perhaps a Bithynian bishop (Eusebius of Nicomedia?) writing to a pope; 'cognitus' may be corrupt (for 'cognatus'?). The sentence 'De Patre autem et Filii diceris... superna baculum est ambulare' is corrupt and the rendering is a guess. The Athanasius sentence 'ut quia ipse quidem sempiternus est...' breaks off incomplete. 17.1: 'Omnium ergo suorum quis Pater esto' is corrupt and only partly rendered; the seal comparison is textually unsure. 18.1: 'fincta' read as 'ficta'; the clause beginning 'Sed et Filius libentissime' lacks a main verb, and the following passage on the sun appears to switch to anti-pagan material, possibly a different source joined by the palimpsest.

18.2: quotations from Hilary (De Trinitate 12), Phoebadius (Contra Arianos) and Ambrose (De fide). 'nec sine tuo' read as 'without your own [Son]'; 'etenim huic illorum initio nescio quis tertius Deus' is elliptical, probably corrupt. 'initium non caret' is illogical in context; the sense seems to require 'has a beginning' (or 'initio non caret'). 19.1: the Constantine passage is garbled ('per fidem sine fide possidentur', 'daturam', 'polliceri'); translated by evident sense, uncertain. 'in libro levitis' probably for 'a libro'/'apud levitas'. 20.1 and 21.1 are an Old Latin version of the Ascension of Isaiah (chs. 2-3, 7). Bechira = Belchira; Beliac = Beliar; Asamar and Medor (Media?) unclear; Ochodiam 'king of Gomorrah' is the text's reading. 'domine rex quoniam galea grec...' is too damaged to construe. In 21.1 'Et dixit' at Isaiah's question should evidently be 'dixi'; 'susus' = 'sursum'; 'ex qua oculum factum' = 'ex quo saeculum factum'; 'qualis ad dextram' read with sense 'not such as'; 'Hilariter ... tu...' fragmentary; 'Cum enim sustuleris te' probably for 'sustulero'.

nodes.text: THE MOST ANCIENT FRAGMENTS OF ARIAN SERMONS
FOUND ON REUSED PARCHMENTS AND NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME WITH SUITABLE REFUTATIONS.
(Mai, Collectio, vol. III, part II, p. 208.)
FIRST FRAGMENT.

Recently, dearest brother, you judged that I should be told about the slanderers who speak against our faith, which is the true one, saying: "How do you say that there is one God, and then again assert that he has a son, Christ? Necessarily, if God has a son, he also has a wife, or else he is certainly female, and conceived and bore a son from somewhere else. See, you are now saying there are several gods; how can you mock us because we say that there are gods?"

We have learned from you that the sacrilegious raise these objections against us. For this reason we have thought it necessary both to meet their error and to instruct your holiness about our hope, which we carry. For we could no longer refuse, since your holiness desired to receive a written instruction in the true faith: yet not from ourselves, but according to the tradition of the divine Scriptures, through the grace of God almighty, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the ministry of the Holy Spirit, who distributes graces without hesitation to those who believe in God through Christ. So we have ventured, trusting in your prayers, and judging that your holiness's desire is also good; which, with the Lord's assent, we have hastened to satisfy, dearest brother: since, with you suggesting it rather often and pressing it quite frequently, we could no longer pretend not to notice: trusting not in loftiness of speech or in the wording of a polished discourse, for which we have had no training at all; but taking refuge in the mercy of the Lord, to whose glory we have resolved to speak, believing him who said: Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it. And again, as the prophet says: The Lord will give the word to those who bring good news with great power. And again: It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father. So the insults of the sacrilegious have moved us too to speak, and the persistence of your charity has also compelled us. And he who gave the mouth for speaking is able to supply us also with the word through your prayers, so that, strengthened by his grace, we may speak fittingly for the common benefit and to the glory of the same maker of our nature. For the holy and divine Scriptures, having deep and boundless treasures within them, shining [as they are], need nothing further; as the Lord says: Search the Scriptures, since you think that in them you have eternal life. And these are what bear witness about me. And you do not wish to come to me, that you may have eternal life? And again: Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. And our Lord Jesus Christ says this too: I am the light of this world: whoever follows me does not remain in darkness, but will have the light of life. Him the holy prophets proclaimed the sun of righteousness. So this is the sun of righteousness, Christ the Son of God. This is the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world; which the darkness did not overcome. This [light] shines in pure hearts, and is seen by the clear eye of the mind in the only-begotten's own singular and incorruptible nature; and he shows most plainly to all who desire it the knowledge of the one true God, saying to the Jews: How can you believe, receiving glory from one another? and you do not seek the glory from the one God. And again he says to the Father: The hour has come; glorify your Son, so that the Son may also glorify you; as you have given him power over all flesh, that to all whom you have given him he may give eternal life. And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent. So it is necessary for those who wish to be Christians to know the one true God, who alone is without beginning, unbegotten; and his only-begotten Son, in his own proper and singular begotten nature, true God, obedient and subject in will and nature to the unbegotten God, his Father. Since, then, we have spoken of one true God according to the tradition of the Scriptures, just as, according to true reason, there is one true God, one king, one lord, one creator and maker of the universe: since, then, he alone, without beginning, possesses supreme power, he alone needs nothing, he alone is not under another's law nor awaits a command; he alone has no superior, just as he has made no one his equal; he who is wholly unborn God made the Son wholly born, through whom he created all things, as it is written: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made: creator [made] a creator, God [made] God, subject to all creation [as its God] and obedient in all his commands. This [Son] did not advance afterwards, but was at once perfect, as we have said: [God,] as far as he was able, sealing all power and all wisdom in the establishment of the Son, as it is written: whom God the Father has sealed. Hence too the Apostle proclaims him the image of the invisible God, since God shows his invisible power or wisdom in the substance of the Son. Therefore God showed in the Son as much as he could in power and wisdom: whence the Apostle teaches that the Son is the power of God and the wisdom of God: not, then, that power or wisdom without beginning which is in the invisible God; but [the one] seated at the right hand of God, so that he should be receiving from the Father, the Son of God's love, whom God loves. He cheated him of nothing, to whom he handed over all things, as the Gospel proclaims: The Father loves the Son, and has handed all things into his hand. And the Son, receiving all things from the Father, above all, before all, with all, worships the Father. Him, then, we accept through the Scriptures as God of all creation: born, subject to the unborn God; born lord of all creation, but minister of the unborn Lord; born king of all creation, under the power of the unborn king; born true light, subject to the unborn, inaccessible light; born wisdom, obedient in all things to the only wise, unborn [God]; born creator under the unborn creator; good shepherd of all creation, born lamb of the unborn God; born life, giving life to all creation at the Father's will, subject to the only living God without beginning, as the Son says: As the Father has life in himself — he has it and did not receive it — so he has also given the Son to have life in himself, incomparable in his own born substance; just as the Father is recognised to be incomparable in his unborn substance. So we confess one and one God, not two Gods: for we do not say two unborn, or two fathers....
FRAGMENT II.

... the benefits of Christ, assisting the prayer of believers, and interceding for them with unutterable groanings, and leading the saints to the Son, to be brought through the Son to the Father. As the holy apostle Paul says: No one can say "Lord Jesus" except in the Holy Spirit. And the Son indicates: No one can come to the Father except through me. It is necessary, then, for us to confess this trinity. The Holy Spirit magnifies the Son, as the Son says: He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you. And the Son glorifies the Father, as he says: I have glorified you on earth; I have made your name known to the people whom you gave me. This Spirit, then, remains in all the saints, as the Son said: I will ask my Father, and he will give you another advocate, to be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, since it does not see him nor know him: but you recognise him, because he remains with you and is in you. So he remains, as we have said, in all the saints, not divided but whole: for that nature cannot be divided: for what is not composed of members cannot be divided either, but continues whole in all. For we do not call the Holy Spirit God, because Scripture does not either; but [we call him] subject to God the Son, and obedient in all things to the commands of that Son, as the Son [is] to the Father. And just as the Father sealed all power and all wisdom and goodness in the establishment of the Son, so too the Son, at the Father's command, displayed all power and all wisdom in the Holy Spirit. So in that Holy Spirit archangels and angels, and all spiritual powers, and all the saints worship the Son, and through the Son the Father. For thus the Son too, after the resurrection, handing on the saving mystery of the Trinity to his disciples, says: All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go, teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you: and see, I am with you all days until the end of the age.
FRAGMENT III.

.... the Father [is] unique, a simple Spirit, alone good, alone having immortality and dwelling in inaccessible light; so too the Son is unique in his only-begotten nature, which he received from the Father. He is better, by an incomparable eminence, than all things that were made after him and through him by the providence of God, so that none of the things that were made through him can be compared to him; because he is God of all, giving life to all things by the will of the Father. He is not compared to his Father, from whom he obtained that he should be the life of all; nor, as we have said, could anything else be compared to him, of the things that obtained through him, by the will of God, that they should exist and live. First of these is the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, made by the providence of God through Christ, better and greater than all the others, [who] is declared in the holy Scriptures to be in the third place, after the Father and after the Son. This Spirit, in the third place, is recognised as unique and alone in his uniqueness. Such a one could neither be compared to Christ the Son of God, the maker of his nature, nor is anything of the others, who received through him by the providence of God that they should exist, compared to him: for he is a unique sanctifying power. This Spirit is not God nor Lord, since he is not creator either; for he did not make anything of the things that were not so that they should exist, nor can he make [it]; since he is not God, but the minister of Christ, the Son of his God: ministering in this, that he should sanctify the rational beings which were made through Christ by the will of God, and enlighten [them], and teach [them], and remind [them] to keep the commands of Christ, and distribute grace to all believers. He helps the weakness of our prayer, and pleads for us with groanings that cannot be told, and at Christ's bidding forgives the sins of the penitent, and leads [them] to the true and certain knowledge of Christ. He does not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak, and he teaches, and announces things to come to believers. He professes that Christ is his Lord and God, saying: The Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet. And again the same Spirit says to Christ his God: Your throne, God, [is] for ever and ever; the rod of equity [is] the rod of your kingdom; you have loved justice...
FRAGMENT IV.

.... that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me the command, so I do. So that which has been said rather often, I in the Father and the Father in me, signifies not one substance but two, the unbegotten [substance] of the Father and the only-begotten [substance] of the Son; and therefore the Son is understood [to be] in the bosom of the Father, which is perceived in the love and in the power of him who holds all things: but he himself is infinite: he also holds the other within his embrace. The other, however, receiving from the Father power over all things that were made after him and through him, holds the universe within his embrace. So the Father and the Son are not one and the same: the one who embraces, and the one who is embraced; the unbegotten, and the only-begotten; the begetter, and the one who was begotten; the one who commands, and [...] good, and alone having immortality, and dwelling in inaccessible light. So he alone in his uniqueness is such, and there is no other such God without beginning, both all-holding and sole author of all things. The Son of God too is God, only-begotten by nature, true [and] unchangeable by the will of God his Father, but only-begotten, created and made and begotten by the unbegotten God, God of all things that were made after him and through Jesus by the providence of God his Father. But the Father is God even to the Son, of whom he is also the author, and of all things; and therefore [he is] the only true God, because he is God of God, and holds the Son in his power, and has subjected all things under his feet, according to the Apostle, and has given him the name which is above every name. And therefore the Father [is] one God, who received neither power nor existence from another, but is what he was without beginning, unbegotten, all-holding God. Him, therefore, the holy Scriptures declare one God and Lord, and one good, and alone having immortality, and dwelling in inaccessible light. Not because the Son is not God nor Lord, but because the Father is God even to the Son, and of all things; while the Son is only-begotten God and Lord of all things that were made through him, and good, and kind, and also immortal and unchangeable by nature. But all these things he obtained from the Father, and he is found obedient in all things to his God and Father. So the Father and the Son are not called one God, but the Father alone is called one God, who is God both to the Son, as has been said, and to all: but the Son is not God to the Father, but the Son is Lord and God to all creation: but he worships the Father, and asks [of him], and honours [him], and gives thanks, and is [his] debtor, because he declares that he lives on account of him, and boasts that he has received from him all power in heaven and on earth, according to the gospel tradition, where Jesus is reported saying to the Samaritan woman: We worship what we know, but you worship what you do not know. And the gospel tradition often shows Christ praying to his Father; and it shows him giving thanks to his Father and saying: I thank you, Father, because you have heard me, and I know that you always hear me. So he always worships, because he professes that the Father always hears him. Note, then, the sense of the gospel, that Jesus gives thanks openly for the sake of those who stood by; as he himself declares, saying to his Father: For I know that you always hear me; but I say [this] for the sake of those who stand by, that they may perceive that you have sent me. So attend with care, and see the saving tradition, that Christ wants what he is to be known, [and] what he is not not to be said: for whoever calls Christ what he is not, perverts the knowledge of him who is. So do not go astray: for those who declare the Father to be one and the same as Jesus Christ, [though he is] greater, do not know his Father, according to the saying of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who says: If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father, since my Father is greater than I. With this knowledge, then, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, we ought to seek with care this dwelling in the tabernacle of the Lord, which is promised in the present psalm, and rest on his holy mountain: since the soul that is without stain can walk that way which leads to the heights, of which we treated above, and with a clear and single eye can both make that journey and always gaze upon the good things that have been prepared, according to what has been said: Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. It also always sees God, the giver of good things, as has been said: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. This, then, is what has been said: he who enters without stain and works justice. He has taught what sort of person he ought to be who hastens to the possession of the good things that have been prepared in heaven: then he hands on the commandments like steps, since those who climb up high are seen to climb by steps; and first climbing onto the nearest step, one goes on to the next: then to the third and the fourth, until one reaches the goal, which one cannot do without toil. So those who desire to lay hold of a dwelling in the heights ought to press on with the toils and sweat of godliness with all eagerness, so that they may reach the goal. So, after the soul has been made spotless by the knowledge of godliness, those who desire to make the journey of him who leads into the heights ought to adorn and furnish it with good works; according to what has been said: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. According to this sequence the Lord, answering, sets out what sort of person he who desires to dwell in the heights ought to be, or what he should do, saying: He who enters without stain and works justice, speaking truth in his heart. Further, in this too he teaches in sequence, in order, that he should first establish the truth in himself and in his heart, and should prove it as though putting down a root, so that he may be found just according to the Apostle's teaching, which says thus: With the heart one believes unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. And therefore he says: Speaking truth in his heart, who did no deceit with his tongue. For he who desires heavenly good things ought not to speak deceit; nor to tell whatever he pleases, but to send forth through his lips the truth, searched out and tested in the heart, for salvation both for himself and for those who hear. For the apostle too, teaching this, says: Let no evil word come out of your mouth, but whatever is good for the building up of faith, that it may give grace to those who hear. For it happens that from what someone says carelessly, without concern, he harms his neighbour's soul: and therefore he who wishes to dwell in heaven ought to guard and measure his words; as has been said in the hundred and eleventh psalm: Pleasant is the man who has mercy and lends, he will order his words with judgement. And the Lord Jesus, teaching in the Gospel, says: By your word it is clear that, [speaking] justly without deceit and hypocrisy, you will be justified; and by your word it is clear that, [speaking] deceitfully and wickedly, you will be condemned. For this reason we are taught to guard and measure our words, so that we may teach our neighbour. Desiring to enter the tabernacle of the Lord, we shall do no evil to our neighbour either in word or in deed, according to what has been said: and did no evil to his neighbour. Moreover, he who desires to attain that blessed life ought to keep those he has around him instructed in the Lord's discipline, lest he receive reproach from anyone on their account. For people are accustomed, when they see some who are untaught and undisciplined, to reproach those who have them about them or under them. For in truth it is a reproach to those who ought to instruct, if those who are under their hand are found wanton or undisciplined; because they are held too little to discipline, as has been said: an untaught son [is] a reproach to his father. So this word teaches those who desire....
FRAGMENT V.

[...] of the deity they did not see, but [...] they saw with fleshly eyes, and in [...] and he himself [...] as this word asserts: Whoever has seen me has also seen the Father who sent me. According to [...] therefore [...] err [...]: if anyone has seen the Son in a human body, he supposes the Father too to be bodily; which is a horrible impiety. For according to the true sense, if they are willing to accept this, whoever has seen the Son sent by the Father and carrying out the Father's commands, he has seen the Father, that is, has known [him] [...] are light [...] not. For if anyone [has seen] the Son of God, that is Jesus, in his own unique nature and dignity, which he received when begotten by the Father, and [...] the Jews [...] asserting [...] the Father and the Son named by [...] names, from what has been said above, he indeed in the light of God [...] to the Jews often mentioned, according to [...] the prophet [...]: Behold, I will lay in Zion a stone of outpouring and a rock of stumbling, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. And again: Whoever falls on this stone is broken to pieces; but on whomever it falls, it will crush him. And again: Behold, this one is set for the fall and the rising of many. It is clear, then, that [he is set] for the rising of believers, who will not be put to shame; but for the fall of those who will not believe, who take offence at his teaching along with the Jews, not handling [it] rightly: they themselves will be crushed. Those, then, who saw the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, saw him in two ways: with fleshly eyes they saw a human body, but with the eye of the mind they knew through his works God, the Son of God. When, therefore, he says: Whoever has seen me has also seen the Father who sent me, it means this: that whoever has seen the works of the Son, and through the works has known the power of [his] divinity, has himself seen, that is, has known, him who sent me and commanded me these works, or rather who works through me. Those, then, who saw [become] seeing: enlightened and instructed by the Son, they knew and saw the Father who sent him; according to the assertion of the Son himself, who says.....
FRAGMENT VI.

..... or have had the intention of doing [it], they cannot be advanced by God. But they have added to themselves almost fifty other questions, most empty and most useless, which do not lead them to the kingdom of God and of his Christ, but plunge them into the depths of Gehenna. But let us return to the point from which we digressed. Our case is chiefly against those who call themselves orthodox, who have seized our churches and hold them in tyrannical fashion, saying that the Son is equal in all things and in every respect to God the Father, and that the Holy Spirit is equal in all things and in every respect to God the Father and God the Son: and this very assertion of theirs is one of their nearly thirty sects. And that the Son did not call himself equal to the Father, but affirmed that he was in accord with the Father, the Son himself has disclosed to us, saying: Whoever does not glorify the Son does not glorify the Father who sent him. For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself; and he has given him power to execute judgement. As if he had said: God unbegotten, my begetter, who is and was God without beginning, living, mighty, good, wise, perfect, everlasting, who is without beginning and without end, willed me before all things to be living, mighty, good, wise, perfect, everlasting (we call the Son everlasting in this sense, that although the Son has a beginning, he will nevertheless not have an end, but will remain for ever, and will give everlastingness to all other good beings). And he bestowed on me, in whom he willed me to be, such capacity that I could fulfil all his wishes and dispositions and commands: and so I have fulfilled and always fulfil [them]. For by the Father's will and command I created countless living spirits, everlasting powers and dominions; and the Holy Spirit himself too, who is before all things and greater than all created beings, and the other things heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible, times and ages, I created by the Father's will and command: and there was no discord between the Father commanding and me accomplishing; but just as the Father willed, determined, [and] commanded me, so I too, willing and able, without any hindrance or discord accomplished all things: and also all the other things that were done afterwards, whether the flood, or the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all the other things that are continually done and governed, at the Father's command, because he is the Son of Man. Do not marvel at this, for the hour will come in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of judgement. As if he had said: Do not be unbelieving because you see that I am flesh, and think that I am only a man: for all of you who think that I am only a man will see that I am not only the living God, but also the one who gives life to all the dead; and the just, good, and faithful entering into eternal glory; but the wicked and impious, thieves and robbers, and those who distrusted the truth but believed iniquity, who rejected my teaching and set up their own, will by command of my Father, through me, be sent by my angels into the furnace of eternal fire. Our Lord and God Jesus Christ, the Son of God the Father almighty, has made plain to us more clearly than light what he had said above: Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself unless he has first seen the Father doing [it]; for whatever the Father does, the Son does the same. Likewise, the Son presumes nothing for himself, but does all that the Father commands.

Let us again say a few things against the Macedonians, who say that the Son is like the Father in all things and in every respect, and that there is no difference between the Father and the Son; and against those who call themselves orthodox, who with deadly effect maintain that the Son is equal to God the Father in all things and in every respect: for concerning the Father and the Son they agree, and concerning the Holy Spirit they disagree; because these [the orthodox] make the Holy Spirit too co-equal with the Father and the Son in all things and in every respect, while the Macedonians maintain that the Holy Spirit was created by the Father's command through the Son, and preach that he is the messenger and minister of the Father, as we also [do]. (The treatise ends here, as the empty space on the page shows.)
FRAGMENT VII.

FIRST CHAPTER OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH.

We confess, we believe, we hold that God the Father almighty is without beginning, unbegettable, indivisible, unalterable and unchangeable, supreme, most high, incomparable, and God of all; and that knowing, able, willing, before all ages and times, and before absolutely all things, he created, founded, begot, made the Son for himself: and the Son himself remains indivisible, unchangeable, with God the Father in everlasting ages without end. And that, by the will and decision and command of God the Father almighty, through the only-begotten Son, God, the Holy Spirit [and] all the other things heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible, created, made, born, founded, established, formed, fashioned, came into being. And that the Son in the beginning, and before he descended into the virgin Mary, was always obedient to God his Father. And that, by the disposition and decision of God the Father almighty, through the Son all the prophets, inspired, said that the Son himself would come, to be sent by God the Father as enlightener and Saviour of the human race: and that he would take from the Virgin a temple, that is, flesh, so that the Son of almighty God, because of the assumption of flesh, should be proclaimed Son of man and man, that is, Son of David, because he received flesh from his seed. And that, God the Father sending [him], the Son came into this world, so that through his teaching and passion and death on the cross, and resurrection on the third day, and ascension into heaven with the flesh to the place from which he had descended without flesh: so that through the good of baptism he might save the whole race of men who believe in him with entire faith, whom he also named the Church. And that our Lord and God Jesus Christ taught this on earth, according to what God the Father commanded him in heaven. And that the Son is high priest to God the Father, and mediator between God the Father almighty and every creature: and that he is the one through whom we have been reconciled to God the Father. We believe also that the Son makes request of his Father: he also asks and prays for all the saints and penitents: and that the Son gave and gives thanks to God his Father: and that the prayers and thanksgivings of all are offered to God the Father through the Son: and that, at the command of God the Father, his Son sits at his right hand, and intercedes with his Father for us: and we believe that God the Father has subjected absolutely all things to the Son. And if God the Father subjected all things to the Son, he subjected the Holy Spirit too. But if the Holy Spirit is not subject to the Son, God the Father almighty did not subject all things to his Son. And that too which is written: The Father subjected to the Son; he loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand; and, All things have been handed over to me by my Father; we believe to be thus: in that the Father begot the Son, he said to him, Know that you will create all things, govern [them], and rule over all, as I shall will, decide, command you. And the Son too most gladly [shows] this very thing, that he neither is from himself nor does anything [of himself], but without doubt shows God's workmanship in his nature of brightness, displaying his ministry together with the other created things, serving men by God's providence, like a giant exulting, running his way from the East to the West, bringing to all the light of the brightness of his nature; so that every man who has rational understanding, looking at him, may give thanks to God, who prepared his brightness for the light of human life. For when you see some man preparing a light late at night, do you give thanks to that light according to the reckoning of justice? No, but to him who prepared the light. According to this reckoning of justice, then, or using natural understanding, you ought to magnify only the maker and giver of this; and you will have to give thanks to him who granted you the sight of this light; so that you too, just as the sun shows you the ministry of service according to God's providence, things of which you are a debtor, may render thanksgivings to your giver, who, establishing the sun for your benefit, set it in the heaven, so that it may shine upon the earth. So it is, then, as was said: In the sun he set his tabernacle; and he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, exulted as a giant to run his way: from the highest heaven is his going forth, and his course reaches to its height; and there is none who can hide from his heat. You, therefore, if, remaining in the ignorance of your error, you deny that this creation which is seen is the workmanship of one God, and according to the impiety of your foolishness affirm it to be the work of many gods, who do not exist, the creation itself, by the appearance of its nature, most evidently refutes the foolishness of your error; since it keeps order among its parts, and observes what is proper to the seasons, and [its parts] succeed one another, and as if from unanimity, according to the providence of one God, it displays the use of its ministry to men. It is manifest, therefore, that he who created the heaven also created the lights in the heaven; he also created the earth, and all things which are upon the earth. Likewise in Deuteronomy: And not to you alone do I establish this covenant and these curses, but also to those who are with you today in the sight of the Lord your God, and to those who are not with you today. Likewise in Deuteronomy: And all the nations of the earth will say: Why has the Lord done thus to this land? What is this great wrath of fury? And they will say: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord God of their fathers, which he established for their fathers when he led them out of the land of Egypt. And they went and served foreign gods, and worshipped those whom they had not known, and did not remain with the Lord their God. And the Lord, angered with fury against that land, brought upon it all the curses of the covenant which are written in this book. And the Lord removed them from their land in fury and wrath and very great exasperation, and cast them into another land; and so on. This divine law, these holy Scriptures, Constantine the elder defended, saying: "Although I perceive myself to be most exalted and lord of all, I know that I am mortal, and I understand that at some time I shall leave the glory of this kingdom." Eternal fame, therefore, is to be sought, and those exalted things which descend from the eternal Lord and the exalted God; which the divine laws promise; which the sacred [words] of the Son of God pledge; which after the course of this life are bestowed by the Son of God himself as guarantor. Let the glory of this brief time therefore be laid aside, that [those things] may be possessed through faith, [...] which he himself, according to the sacred law of God, promises: immortality without end, to be given after the bond of death, after a very brief life; and so on. And it happened, when Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians had come, and had taken Samaria, and had led away [...] said [...] into prison, and had brought them to Mount Medor [...] to the river Gozan, Bechira was a young man, and fled and came to Jerusalem in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah: he did not walk in [...] of Samaria his father, because he feared Hezekiah. And he was found in the time of Hezekiah speaking words of injustice in Jerusalem, and [...] by the servants [...] in the region of Bethlehem. And Bechira despised Isaiah and the prophets who were with him, saying that Isaiah and the prophets who are with him prophesied in Jerusalem [...] of the city of Judea, that they are being abandoned, and against the sons of Judea and [...] that they are led captive. And then, lord king, that [...] you will be led away through iron: they prophesied in Israel and in Judah and in Jerusalem; and Isaiah himself said that he prophesied more than Moses. For Moses said that a man cannot see God; but Isaiah said: I saw God, and behold, I live. Understand, king, that he is a liar: and behold, he called Jerusalem Sodom, and the princes of Judea and Jerusalem he named the people of Gomorrah. And when he had disparaged Isaiah and the prophets in many things, Beliar also settled in the heart of Manasseh, and in the hearts of the princes of Judah and Benjamin, and of the eunuchs and the king's counsellors. FRAGMENT XXI.

[...] sons to the voice of Micaiah and the other prophets, saying in it, in which you heard my prophecy: I saw a glorious angel, not according to the glory of the angels whom I always used to see, but having a great and holy brightness, which brightness I cannot describe. And he came near and took my hand, and I said: Who are you, and what is your name, and where are you taking me? For I had received strength to speak with him. And he said to me: When I have lifted you up and shown you the vision, for which I have been sent to you, then you will understand who I am; but I will not tell you my name, because you are to return into the flesh. For when you have been lifted up, then you will see. For this I have been sent, that I may come. He answered me simply and said to me: And you will see one greater than me. He speaks cheerfully, simply [...] of those greater than himself he will see. For this I have been sent from the seventh heaven, that I may show you all things. And he lifted me up, and I myself ascended into the first firmament, and there I saw Samael and his might: and there was a great war in it, and the angels of Satan envying one another; for as above, so also on earth. And I said to the angel who was with me: What is this war, and what is this envy? And he said to me: Thus it has been from when the world was made until now, and thus the war will be until he comes whom you are to see, and he will purge it. And afterwards he set me above the firmament; and it was heaven, and I saw there a throne in the middle, and to its right and to its left were angels; the angels on the left [were not] such as those on the right: for those on the right had great brightness, and all praised with one voice; and the throne was in the middle, and those on the left blessed after [them]. And there was a voice from the left, not like [theirs], nor was it less similar to them; and I asked the angel who was leading me, and said to him: To whom do the angels send hymns?
